LNG, mining & large projects · Mozambique

Land around LNG sites, mines and large projects, mapped from the air

Around a large project the land changes faster than anywhere on the route. We map the structures, excavations, tracks and cleared ground inside and around your site, concession and resettlement villages, compare them between dated surveys, and deliver a register your land, social-performance and security teams can act on. A person reviews every result.

Send us your site boundary Resettlement baselines

The problem

The land around a large project does not stand still

A new plant, a mine or a resettlement programme changes the land around it: roads open, people move towards work and services, and the edges of the site become the busiest ground in the district.

Settlement at the fence

Houses, stalls and yards grow along access roads and against site fences, inside the safety and exclusion zones your engineers have drawn.

Excavations at the concession edge

Pits, spoil heaps and new tracks appear inside and around a mining right, and the new Mining Law reserves areas for artisanal and small-scale mining that can sit right beside it.

Villages that keep changing

Resettlement villages and the land around them change after the move. The rights holder carries the cost of resettlement, and the question of what was there at the cut-off date keeps coming back.

Under the Petroleum Law, the rights holder bears the costs of resettlement after prior consultation, and the people affected must be given condições de vida condignas e superiores, living conditions that are dignified and better than before (Lei n.º 8/2026, art. 61). The Mining Law approved in May 2026 sets aside a share of mining revenue for community funds and reserves areas for artisanal and small-scale mining (AIM, 8 May 2026). Both put the land around a project, and the record of what stood where and when, under closer attention.

Who this is for

  • Land and resettlement managers
  • Social-performance and community-relations teams
  • HSE managers who own safety and exclusion zones
  • Mine planning, closure and rehabilitation teams
  • Asset-protection teams, as recipients of flagged areas
  • Lenders and independent monitors
  • ESIA and RAP consultancies

LNG and gas plants

Around the plant, its roads and its resettlement villages

Mozambique’s onshore LNG plants are being built on the Afungi peninsula in Palma district. Mozambique LNG announced the full restart of its onshore and offshore activities on 29 January 2026 and expects first LNG in 2029 (TotalEnergies). Rovuma LNG selected its engineering, procurement and construction contractor in August 2026, with a final investment decision aimed for 2026 (ExxonMobil).

Around sites like these, the line becomes a boundary and the question becomes a ring. We map what stands inside the site or licence area, in a band around it and inside the safety and exclusion zones you define, each structure listed with its distance to the boundary or the source. Re-surveys then show how settlement grows around the plant, along its access roads and in and around the resettlement villages. During construction, dated drone orthophotos show earthworks and laydown progress, and inventories of tanks, containers and plant record what the imagery shows on each survey date.

What you receive

  • Structures inside and around the site, with an optional setback inside the fence
  • Structures inside the safety and exclusion zones you define
  • Settlement growth around the plant and its roads
  • A cut-off-date register with reviewer categories
  • Re-surveys of resettlement villages and their buffers
  • Construction and earthworks progress between dates

In the north

Satellite work needs no one on site, so a baseline can start where access is restricted. Results go only to the contacts you name, and we never publish maps of your site or the settlements around it without your written permission. Any drone or ground element has to fit the project’s own security arrangements, the operator’s permission and the Defence authorisation for the survey.

Mining concessions

Concession edges, excavations and hazard zones

Mozambique’s large mines sit in provinces where access can change quickly: graphite at Balama, where force majeure was declared in December 2024 because site access could not be secured during post-election unrest and lifted by July 2025 (African Mining Market); rubies near Montepuez; coal at Moatize in Tete. A register built from the air keeps working when the road to site does not.

For a concession we map the structures inside the boundary and in a ring around it, the pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps and water-filled excavations inside and around the mining right, and the new tracks that reach them, with new sites flagged between dates. We list the structures inside the zones your engineers define, such as tailings dam-break inundation areas and blast exclusion zones, each with its distance to the source.

What you receive

  • Structures inside and around the concession boundary
  • Artisanal excavations and disturbed ground, with new sites between dates
  • New tracks and access routes into the concession
  • Structures in tailings, blast and other hazard zones you define
  • Revegetation on rehabilitated land, tracked between dates
  • Stockpile and earthworks volumes from drone elevation models, subject to permits

Resettlement

A dated record before the census, at the cut-off date and after

Mozambique’s resettlement regulation starts with identifying and delimiting the area, counting the families affected and recording its current occupation, and asks for at least four public consultations (Decreto n.º 31/2012, arts. 19 and 23). Lenders add IFC Performance Standard 5: a census and a cut-off date for eligibility. The client “is not required to compensate or assist those who encroach on the project area after the cut-off date for eligibility, provided the cut-off date has been clearly established and made public” (PS5, para. 23).

We count and map the structures in the project area on set dates: before the census to size it, on the cut-off date as a dated record, and after it to show what has appeared since. The census, the consultations and the eligibility decisions stay with your resettlement team.

Drones near large sites

Where a drone helps, and where it cannot go

Dated drone orthophotos and elevation models give the detail for construction progress, rehabilitation and volumes, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires. In Mozambique that means IACM approval of the operation, the Minister of National Defence’s authorisation of the survey and authorisation to release its data (Lei n.º 6/2024, art. 13). Afridrone is working towards the operator approvals Mozambique requires.

Sites a drone may not overfly

Lei n.º 6/2024 restricts aircraft operations within at least 5 km of strategic national-security areas (art. 11(1)), and strategic petroleum areas are under a special protection regime (Lei n.º 8/2026, art. 6(1)). IACM’s directive allows no flights over places of strategic interest or military installations, and mine blasting areas need the managing agency’s written permission.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, excavations, tracks and cleared ground inside and around your site
  • Measure each one to your boundary, zone or source
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Deliver dated, credited records that support your resettlement, engagement and legal processes

What we don’t do

  • Provide security, guarding or response services
  • Identify, count or follow people or vehicles
  • Model tailings, blast or flood zones: your engineers define them
  • Replace the resettlement census, consultations or statutory surveys

Frequently asked questions

Can you start without anyone travelling to the site?

Yes. A satellite-based survey starts from your site or concession boundary and dated imagery, with no one on site and no drone flight. That is the practical first step where access is slow, costly or restricted, including in the northern provinces.

Who sees the maps of our site and the settlements around it?

Only the contacts you name. We never publish maps of a client’s site, concession or resettlement villages, or of the settlements around them, without written permission.

Do you map artisanal mining on our concession?

We map what the imagery shows inside and around your mining right, such as pits, disturbed ground, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations and new tracks, and flag new sites between dates. We do not identify or follow the people working there, and whether an activity is authorised is for you and the authorities to decide.

Can a drone fly near an LNG plant or a mine?

Only with the operator’s permission and the authorisations for that flight. Lei n.º 6/2024 restricts aircraft operations within at least 5 km of strategic national-security areas, IACM’s directive allows no flights over places of strategic interest, and mine blasting areas need the written permission of the agency that manages them. Around such sites, satellite work usually comes first.

Can you track the progress of construction or rehabilitation?

Yes. Dated drone orthophotos and elevation models, compared side by side, show where ground has been cut or filled and where earthworks and laydown areas have grown. On rehabilitated land and closed borrow pits we track revegetation between dates. Drone work is subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires.

Do you replace our resettlement census?

No. A dated register supports the census and asset inventory and your IFC Performance Standard 5 cut-off-date records. The census, the consultations and the eligibility decisions stay with your resettlement team.

Send us your site or concession boundary

The boundary as KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile or GeoPackage, the zones your engineers use and the dates that matter. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
